chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
title: Leonard Feather and wealthy Bobby Burnet form a small group
summary: At the Rhythm Club Feather asked him to join a mixed combination with trumpeter Bobby Burnet, a young millionaire who dressed like a tramp.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I was talking about how I was at the Rhythm Club one day, my favorite hangout spot where the musicians gathered to get the gigs and one thing and another, and Leonard Feather walked up to me and asked me would I be interested in working in a small combination with Bobby Burnet, a trumpet player. I told him, 'Well, why not? I'll work with anybody.' So I was introduced to Bobby, and we talked, and he explained what he had. He didn't have much work, but he thought with him and Leonard Feather, they could get something going.
But anyway, they had a week or two engagement at Nick's

in the Village, and we got the band together and rehearsed. I don't remember all of the members of the band, but there was Bobby, he was the trumpet player... Bobby Burnet was the trumpet player, Leonard Feather was the pianist, and Manzie Johnson was the drummer, and I was the saxophonist. Now, there's two that I don't remember, one or two. I don't know if it was a five-piece combination or a six-piece combination.
But you probably had a string bass.
Most likely. But I can't think of who it was.
And this was February to March 1941.
Yes.
So this would be after you had left Russell for another time...
Yeah. No, that was Louis' band I had left. Louis' band. I left him in '40. And this was '41.
Now, who was Bobby Burnet?
Well, Bobby Burnet was a trumpet player. He was a White trumpet player. He used to work with...what's the tenor saxophone player's name? Charlie...?
Ventura?
No, the one that recorded... Charlie,
Charlie, Charlie, Charlie... All these great names; I don't remember the great ones.
A White tenor player?

He was White, yeah. He could blow, too. Oh, he was sensational. Charlie, Charlie, Charlie... In fact, I think Lena Horne worked with him. Either her or Billie Holiday. Geez, how could I forget anybody's name? Charlie, Charlie... A tenor player...
Well, we can come back to it.

Yeah, we can come back to it. We will come back to it. Because you know who I'm talking about. I mean, he was very popular. He was one of the big ones, do you know what I mean? Like Benny Goodman and them. Charlie... It wasn't Charlie Spivak, because he wasn't a tenor player. [CHARLIE BARNET IS THE TENOR PLAYER]
Bobby Burnet apparently was very wealthy.

Well, for them days he was very wealthy. He inherited between seven and eight million dollars in his own right, and he was a young man then. So he was pretty well-to-do. But you would never know it, because he had an old, broken-down, second-hand car and a reversible raincoat that he wore all the time. To me he looked like Pete the Tramp. But he was supposed to be a millionaire, so I guess maybe he was starting off to be eccentric.
